analysis.one_liner: Lets regulators claw back private equity investors' health care profits after patient-harming failures and requires public disclosure of hospital ownership and finances.
analysis.headline: The bill had no cosponsors and was referred to three House committees; no committee has acted on it.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would let the Justice Department and state attorneys general claw back money that private equity investors and executives took out of a health care company—salaries, bonuses, management fees, dividends, and profits—if the company later closes, goes bankrupt, misses payroll, or defaults on loans, and could bring criminal charges. It would also cut off Medicare and Medicaid payments to providers that sell their buildings to real estate investment trusts, repeal tax breaks those trusts get, and require hospitals, health systems, and physician practices to publicly report who owns them, how much debt they carry, and what they pay investors.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients at hospitals and clinics owned by private equity firms and corporate chains, and the workers at those facilities who lose pay when a firm loads a hospital with debt and fees and then fails. The clawed-back money is earmarked for unpaid employee salaries and benefits, pension shortfalls when a firm goes bankrupt, and health care needs in the harmed community. Communities also gain public visibility into who actually owns and profits from their local hospitals and practices.

how_it_helps.text: When a private-equity-owned health care company hits a triggering event—such as bankruptcy, closure, missing payroll for a quarter of its workforce for 90 days, or defaulting on a loan—the bill lets the U.S. Attorney General or state attorneys general claw back compensation, dividends, management fees, and profits the investors took out in the surrounding 10 years, with criminal penalties of 1 to 6 years and civil penalties up to 5 times the clawback amount.

Money recovered is directed to covering unpaid employee salaries and benefits and to serving the health care needs of the harmed community, with pension shortfalls prioritized when the triggering event is bankruptcy.

It ends a special tax rule for REIT subsidiaries that own health care property, removes REIT dividends from the qualified business income deduction, and makes selling health care assets to a REIT or pledging them as REIT loan collateral grounds for exclusion from Medicare and Medicaid—directly attacking the sale-leaseback financing model.

It requires hospitals, health systems, physician practices, hospices, dialysis facilities, and other health care entities to report annually on ownership, debt, leases, dividends to investors, and mergers, with the information posted publicly and penalties up to $5 million per false or missing report.
It directs the HHS Inspector General to study profit-driven practices in health care, including insurers' prior authorization and utilization review practices that restrict or delay care.

analysis.who_pays: Private equity firms, their executives and control persons, and real estate investment trusts that own health care property: they face clawbacks of up to ten years of compensation and profits, criminal penalties, new taxes, loss of Medicare and Medicaid revenue, and mandatory public financial disclosure. Hospital and practice owners also bear reporting compliance costs.
analysis.who_pays_short: Private equity and health care REITs

drawbacks.text: The clawback and criminal provisions reach a wide range of financial outcomes—missed payrolls, missed rent, loan defaults, and bankruptcy—so investors and executives could face penalties of up to five times their compensation even when the triggering event was partly caused by market conditions or the COVID-era financial pressures of running a hospital, though the bill does allow an affirmative defense if the covered party could not have prevented the event.

The bill targets every health care buyer that takes control of a provider, not just firms that gut them, so even well-run acquirers in health care face new federal criminal exposure, mandatory ownership disclosures, and possible loss of Medicare and Medicaid billing if they sell property to a REIT—compliance costs that critics could argue make acquisitions of struggling hospitals less attractive and accelerate closures instead of preventing them.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets a real, documented pattern—private equity takeovers of hospitals and practices followed by asset sales, fees, staff cuts, and sometimes bankruptcy—and gives regulators real tools, including clawbacks of investor pay when a takeover ends in a triggering event and an end to tax breaks that reward selling hospital real estate to REITs. The costs are borne by investors in health care deals; the chief design concern is that the clawback penalty attaches to specific financial outcomes (missed payrolls, closures, bankruptcies) even when a downturn or other causes contributed, though an affirmative defense is available if the covered party could not have prevented the event.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Ways and Means, Judiciary, and Energy and Commerce committees, where no action has been taken.

narrative.text: Rep. Maggie Goodlander introduced the bill on February 12, 2026, and it was referred to the House Ways and Means, Judiciary, and Energy and Commerce committees.
As of the latest record, no other member of the House has signed on as a cosponsor.
The only action recorded beyond introduction is the referral to committee; no hearings, markups, or votes have occurred.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: If the bill stays where it is, private equity firms and REITs keep the current rules that let them extract fees and profits from health care companies without clawback or public disclosure, and nothing changes for patients yet.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Private equity and health care REITs

for.name: Rep. Maggie Goodlander
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and is its only sponsor

sides.party_line_note: The bill has a single Democratic sponsor and no cosponsors of either party, so no bipartisan or bloc-based pattern has formed yet.

industries.industry: Private equity and health care private funds
industries.note: The bill claws back investor compensation, salaries, fees, and profits taken from a health care company that later hits a triggering event, adds criminal exposure of 1–6 years, and lets state attorneys general sue on patients' behalf. It is aimed squarely at the investor playbook of loading up hospitals and practices with debt and fees.

industries.industry: Real estate investment trusts (REITs) in health care
industries.note: Health care providers that sell property to, or borrow from, a REIT would be barred from Medicare and Medicaid, the special tax treatment for REIT health care property is repealed, and REIT dividends lose their qualified business income deduction. Patients benefit because sale-leaseback deals are a known driver of hospital financial distress.

industries.industry: Hospitals, health systems, and corporate-owned physician practices
industries.note: New annual ownership, debt, and fee reporting with public posting and up to $5 million penalties per false report. The industry keeps operating and billing federal programs, but under far more public scrutiny of its finances.

The bill does not directly regulate insurers, but the HHS Inspector General study would evaluate insurer practices like prior authorization that restrict or delay care. Health insurers face potential future exposure depending on the findings.

analysis.trajectory: With zero cosponsors and no committee action beyond referral to three committees—any one of which must act before the bill can move—newly introduced bills at this stage overwhelmingly die quietly in committee. Unless Goodlander builds cosponsor support or leadership takes an interest, the bill is unlikely to reach a floor vote this Congress.
